lead: The month of May closes with the feast of the Visitation. Zephaniah calls Daughter Zion to sing, because the King of Israel, the Lord, is in her midst. In the Gospel Mary, who now carries that Lord within her, goes in haste to Elizabeth. The child in Elizabeth’s womb leaps for joy, and Mary sings the Magnificat.

The responsorial canticle from Isaiah 12 repeats the theme: “Great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.” Instead of Zephaniah, the Mass may use Romans 12:9–16, Paul’s call to sincere love and to rejoicing with those who rejoice: the charity Mary shows in going to serve her kinswoman. The feast replaces the readings of Monday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time.

r.h: The Lord is in your midst
set: Zephaniah prophesied in Judah “in the days of King Josiah” (1:1), in the seventh century before Christ, probably before Josiah’s reform. Most of his book is a stern warning about the “day of the Lord” against the pride and idolatry of Jerusalem and the nations. But the book ends with a promise: a humble and lowly remnant will seek refuge in the Lord (3:12), and the Lord will rejoice over his people.
Our passage is that final song of joy. The mood changes completely: from judgment to celebration, from fear to the presence of God.
str: v. 14: the call to joy: sing, shout, rejoice, O daughter Zion.
v. 15: the reason: the Lord has taken away the judgments; the King of Israel is in your midst.
v. 16: do not fear, O Zion.
vv. 17–18: the Lord, a warrior who gives victory, rejoices over you with singing.
kw: A tender name for Jerusalem and her people, pictured as a young woman. The Church has seen in Mary the Daughter of Zion in person (Lumen Gentium 55).
Used twice (vv. 15, 17). The same Hebrew word can mean “within you”. Christian readers have heard in it a hint of Mary, in whose womb the Lord came to dwell.

The first of four cries of joy in v. 14. The Greek translation begins with chaire, “rejoice”, the same word with which the angel greets Mary in Luke 1:28; many commentators hear an echo of Zephaniah there.
vv: Sing aloud, O daughter Zion; shout, O Israel!
The prophet who warned of the day of wrath ends with a song. God’s last word is not judgment but joy.
The king of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst; you shall fear disaster no more.
The reason for joy is not a change of circumstances but a presence. God himself is with his people.
he will rejoice over you with gladness, he will renew you in his love; he will exult over you with loud singing
Not only the people rejoice in God; God rejoices over his people. He sings over them like a bridegroom or a mother.
ch: The Church reads this song on the feast of the Visitation because it is fulfilled in Mary. The Second Vatican Council calls her the exalted Daughter of Zion, in whom, after the long waiting, the times are fulfilled (Lumen Gentium 55). The Catechism calls her the Ark of the Covenant, the place where the glory of the Lord dwells: she is the dwelling of God among men (CCC 2676). The Lord who was in the midst of Zion is now in the midst of Mary, and she carries him into a house in the hill country.

r.h: The mother of my Lord comes to me
set: The angel Gabriel has told Mary that she will conceive the Son of the Most High, and has given her a sign: her kinswoman Elizabeth, old and called barren, is in her sixth month (1:36). Mary sets out at once. The hill country of Judea lay some days’ walk south of Nazareth. An ancient tradition places Zechariah’s home at Ein Karem, near Jerusalem.

Background. Luke tells the story with echoes of David bringing the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). David asked, “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (6:9); he danced before the Lord; and the ark stayed in the house of Obed-edom three months (6:11). Elizabeth asks a similar question, John leaps for joy, and Mary stays about three months. Many commentators see in this a picture of Mary as the new Ark, carrying the Lord himself.
str: vv. 39–40: Mary goes in haste to the house of Zechariah and greets Elizabeth.
vv. 41–45: the child leaps; Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blesses Mary and her child.
vv. 46–50: the Magnificat, first part: what God has done for Mary.
vv. 51–55: second part: what God does for the lowly and for Israel.
v. 56: Mary stays about three months and returns home.
kw: Not nervous hurry but eager readiness. Mary does not wait to be served as the mother of the Lord; she goes to serve.
The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for the twins struggling in Rebekah’s womb (Genesis 25:22). Here the leap is one of joy (v. 44): the forerunner greets the Lord before either is born.
“My soul magnifies the Lord” (v. 46). To magnify is to make great, to proclaim greatness. Mary does not make God greater; she lets his greatness be seen. The Latin Magnificat gives the song its name.
vv: In those days Mary set out and went with haste to a Judean town in the hill country,
St Ambrose comments that the grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow efforts (in substance). Faith makes Mary set out.
Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.
These words, with the angel’s greeting, form the first part of the Hail Mary. When we pray it, we speak with Gabriel and with Elizabeth.
And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?
“My Lord” is the name of God. Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, confesses that the child in Mary’s womb is the Lord. The Church therefore calls Mary the Mother of God (CCC 495).
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.
The first beatitude in Luke’s Gospel is for faith. Mary is blessed not only because she is the mother but because she believed (CCC 148).
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly;
The song echoes the song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and the psalms. God reverses the world’s order, and the poor of the Lord, the anawim, are lifted up.
ch: The Catechism teaches that John was filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, by Christ himself whom the Virgin Mary had just conceived, and that Mary’s visit to Elizabeth became God’s visit to his people (CCC 717). The Magnificat is the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church (CCC 2619); the Church sings it every evening at Vespers. St Ambrose wrote: let the soul of Mary be in each of us to magnify the Lord, let the spirit of Mary be in each to rejoice in God (in substance).

Pope St John Paul II, in Redemptoris Mater 12, saw in the Visitation Mary’s faith confirmed by Elizabeth’s words and her charity shown in service. The feast is also a feast of human life before birth: two unborn children meet, and one of them is God.

qa: Why do Catholics call Mary “blessed” and honour her so much?

Because Scripture itself says that all generations will call her blessed (1:48), and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, was the first to do it. The honour given to Mary is not worship, which belongs to God alone. It is praise of what God has done in her, and it always leads to him: “the Mighty One has done great things for me”.
Did Mary herself compose the Magnificat?

Luke presents it as Mary’s song, and the Church prays it as hers. Many scholars note that it is woven from Old Testament songs and psalms, and some think Luke drew on a hymn sung by the early Jewish Christians of Jerusalem. Neither view takes anything away from it: a young woman of Israel who knew the Scriptures by heart could pray in their words, as Jesus himself prayed in the words of the psalms.
What does the leaping of John say about the unborn child?

Luke shows an unborn child responding with joy to the presence of the Lord, himself unborn. The Church sees here the dignity of human life from its beginning. The Catechism teaches that human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception (CCC 2270).
rite: The feast of the Visitation was first kept by the Franciscans in the thirteenth century and was extended to the whole Latin Church by Pope Urban VI in 1389. It used to fall on 2 July. Since the reform of the calendar in 1969 it is kept on 31 May, between the Annunciation (25 March) and the birth of St John the Baptist (24 June), so that the order of the Gospel is followed. In many parishes and homes the May devotions to Our Lady end today, often with a procession, the Rosary and the crowning of her statue. The Second Joyful Mystery of the Rosary is this Gospel.
study: Mary went “with haste” to help. Who near me needs a visit or a helping hand this week?
Elizabeth recognised the Lord hidden in Mary. Where is the Lord hidden in the people I will meet today?
Which line of the Magnificat do I most need to make my own prayer, and why?
How does our parish and family protect and welcome life before birth?
